docs.engine.overview: The engine takes a tree of nodes and puts it on the glass. Everything in between is three calls:
```ts
import { mount, attachPainter } from "game-kit"
import { pixiPainter } from "game-kit/pixi"
const host = mount(document.querySelector("#app")!, desk)
const painter = pixiPainter(host.view, host.viewport())
attachPainter(host, painter)
There is no draw call after that: `attachPainter` repaints whenever the host says something
changed — the window resized, the onlooker switched theme, a new tree arrived.
## What happens to one card
Take a `1 × 1.4` card on a 375×812 phone and follow it down to a pixel.
**The host measures the view** and says what a unit is worth: a quarter of the shorter side, so
94 pixels. The card is therefore 94 by 131.6 — and this is the only place in the whole
chain where units become pixels. Nothing is rounded: half a pixel is the honest answer.
**The plan walks the tree** and turns the card into one **quad**: a closed contour as points, the
fill layers, the stroke — all of it already in pixels. Plus a matrix saying where that contour
lands on the glass. The shape itself stays in its own coordinates, around its own origin.
**The painter puts the quad on the canvas.** It adds nothing of its own — only a token name
turned into a colour, because a canvas has no CSS cascade and nothing else can resolve one.
Nobody touched the tree along the way. The plan is built from scratch every frame and remembers
nothing: a node knows what it IS, and not where it is on screen.
## Why a canvas rather than HTML
The desk is a picture. No card on it is an element: it cannot be selected in an inspector, styled
by CSS, or found by a query. Menus and settings AROUND the desk are ordinary HTML and stay so.
The trade was made once, deliberately. A hundred cards mid-flight in HTML are a hundred nodes the
browser lays out, styles and composites every frame, and no arrangement of CSS makes that cheaper.
On a canvas they are a hundred entries in one list, and the cost of a frame stops depending on how
many of them there are.
What it costs is debugging: you cannot look at a card through devtools. So a scene carries layers
of its own — `bounds` shows the boxes, `grid` rules the view in units — and they are a VIEWER
setting rather than state: only whoever switched them on can see them.
## The seam runs along the plan
Everything above the painter is plain arithmetic: pure functions a unit test holds down with no GPU
anywhere. Everything a renderer is free to do its own way is below. That is why Pixi lives in
exactly one file and arrives through its own door (`game-kit/pixi`): importing `pixi.js` reaches
for a canvas context at module load, and re-exporting it from the main entry would drag WebGL into
rules running on a server and into every headless test.
## Notes
- The engine knows no words. A caption arrives already written, on the node that carries it: which
languages exist and where the text is kept belong to whoever assembles the tree.
- There are no game rules either. The kit knows how a thing is owned, placed and drawn, and nothing
about tricks, trumps or turns.
- There is no animation yet — which is why `Bakeable` has to be hung by hand where the engine will
eventually work it out for itself.
docs.engine.chain: Three parts, split by what they OWN. The host owns the view, the painter owns the pixels, and a
plan travels between them. None of the three knows the others' business, and that is not tidiness
for its own sake: while it holds, everything above the painter is checked by a unit test with no
GPU anywhere near it.
## The host owns the view
```ts
const host = mount(container, desk)   // creates a <canvas> inside container
host.view                             // the canvas itself — what a painter is built on
host.viewport()                       // { width, height, dpr }, remeasured on resize
host.unit()                           // what one unit is worth in pixels right now
host.setRoot(next)                    // a different tree in the same view
host.setViewer({ theme: "light" })    // the onlooker's plane
host.onChange(() => {})               // something changed — worth repainting
Two of these are not obvious.
**`setRoot` replaces the TREE, not the canvas.** A move from the server, a save loaded, a spec
edited — that is new data, not a new scene. The temptation to tear the host down and build another
ends badly: a browser hands out about a dozen WebGL contexts and then starts taking the old ones
back, and a scene goes dark for a reason that is nowhere in the code.
**`onChange` is not a game loop.** There is no ticker: a repaint happens when something actually
changed. While nobody touches the tree, the window or the viewer's settings, the engine spends no
frames at all.
## The painter owns the pixels
```ts
interface Painter {
ready: Promise<void>
draw(plan: Quad[], marks: Mark[], theme: ThemeName): void
resize(width: number, height: number): void
destroy(): void
Four members, and that is all. The stock one is built on Pixi, but the kit asks it for nothing
beyond these four — so a second renderer is one file rather than a rewrite.
`ready` exists because a GPU renderer comes up asynchronously. Drawing into it earlier is fine: it
records the plan and puts it on the glass when it arrives. A scene that mounts and paints in the
same breath would otherwise lose its first frame.
`marks` are a second list, not more quads. A quad is a surface somebody authored; a mark is tooling
drawn over it — the grid, the bounds outline. The model does not know they exist, and they are
always on top.
## The plan is what travels between them
A `1 × 1.4` card with the `plate` surface, moved half a unit to the right, on a 375×812 phone.
Here is the entire quad the painter receives:
```js
id: "card",
x: 234.5, y: 406,          // centre, in pixels from the view's top-left
w: 94, h: 131.6,           // the extent; reported for inspection, the contour is drawn
points: [                  // the contour, in the node's OWN coordinates
layers: [{ paint: "panelBg", opacity: 1 }],
stroke: { color: "accent", width: 2.82, alignment: 1, cap: "butt", join: "miter" },
Every number here adds up, and they are worth recomputing.
- `x: 234.5` is `375/2 + 0.5 × 94`: the centre of the view plus half a unit to the right.
- `width: 2.82` is `0.03 × 94`. The `plate` stroke is authored in units, like everything else.
- The first point's `-47` is exactly half the width: the contour is built around its OWN origin,
not around a place on the screen.
- And its `y: -58.28` is `-131.6/2 + 7.52` — half the height less the radius, `0.08 × 94`. The
contour arrives already rounded: a radius is not a field the renderer is left to apply.
And nothing is rounded. `131.6` stays `131.6`: snapping to whole pixels would mean two neighbouring
nodes drifting apart by half a pixel, each in its own direction.
`transform` repeats the centre because this node is only moved. Turn it or scale it and the same
matrix would say so, while the points stayed exactly as they are. Which of the two applies that
matrix — the renderer or us — is what *Baking nodes* is about.
## Notes
- Every length in a plan is pixels. Not only `w`/`h`, but the stroke, the dash pattern, and the
radius already folded into the points.
- Order in the list is paint order. `z` adds up along the owner chain, so a lifted stack lifts
everything in it.
- A colour arrives as a token name, never a value. Only the renderer can resolve one: a canvas has
no CSS cascade to look a variable up in.
docs.engine.sizes: Nothing in the model is in pixels. A card is `1 × 1.4`, a gap is `0.2`, a border is `0.03`. Those
are **units**, and on their own they mean nothing.
The proportion is a real card's: 2.5 by 3.5 inches, the same 1 to 1.4. A unit here is the width of
a card, and everything else is measured with it.
## One unit is a quarter of the shorter side
```ts
host.unit()   // Math.round(Math.min(width, height) * 0.25)
That is the whole rule. Here is what comes out of it:
| screen | unit | card | cards across |
Four cards across the shorter side, on every device — not a coincidence but `1 / 0.25`. That is
what the fraction buys: a hand of cards is readable on a phone and on a laptop because its size is
named not in pixels but in fractions of the one thing both screens agree about — themselves.
A card authored as "90 pixels" is right on exactly one device. Everywhere else it is either
unreadable or a doll's house, and the only fix is a second set of numbers, and then a third.
## Why the shorter side
Turn a 393×852 phone sideways. The shorter side did not change, so the unit is still 98 and the
card is still 98 × 137.2. What changed is that 8.7 cards now fit across instead of 4.0.
The desk got **wider, not bigger**. That is the right answer: turning a phone gives a player more
room, not larger cards. Compute from the width instead and everything on the desk would jump in
size at every rotation.
## The etalon: the same thing, for one onlooker
The fraction is overridden by a viewer setting:
```ts
host.setViewer({ ...viewer, hudUnit: 60 })   // 60 pixels per unit, for THIS onlooker
This is the accessibility knob. An onlooker who finds everything small turns it up — and **not one
size in the model changes**. Only how many pixels a unit buys for them. Two players at one desk
hold two different numbers and look at the same truth; it never travels, because it is the viewer's
plane rather than state.
Absence of the setting is `auto`, and it is genuinely absence rather than a number. A sentinel like
`0` or `-1` would look like a legal value all the way down to the layout, and the confusion would
have to be untangled where only the result is visible.
In a scene's toolbar this switch stands on each canvas separately rather than once per page: the
etalon is a property of a view, and a page may hold several.
## Notes
- Units become pixels once, in the plan. EVERY length is converted: width, height, radius, stroke,
dash step. One length left in units is right on one screen and wrong on the next, and it looks
like a rendering bug rather than an arithmetic one.
- `dpr` is not part of this. Pixel density is the painter's business: it raises the canvas
resolution, while the numbers in a plan stay in CSS pixels.
docs.engine.inheritance: A node holds only what it was authored with. Everything else — what it gets from its owners —
is not stored on it, never travels the wire, and is computed at the moment it is needed.
There is no `parent.*` in the model either. An owner's field is an ordinary field of another
node, and it is reached through the chain.
## An example that works itself out
```ts
const desk = node("desk", Container({ layout: "free" }))
const hand = node("hand", Container({ layout: "row" }), Transformable({ z: 10, angle: 15, scale: 0.5 }))
const card = node("card", Bounded(), Transformable({ z: 2, angle: 15, scale: 0.5 }))
add(desk, hand)
add(hand, card)
const ctx = contextFor(card, host.unit())
resolveZ(ctx)                                          // 12
sumAlongChain(ctx, "Transformable", "angle")           // 30
productAlongChain(ctx, "Transformable", "scale")       // 0.25
Three fields of one atom, and all three combined differently. That is not carelessness: **the
inheritance rule belongs to the FIELD, not to the atom.**
## Five rules
| class | how it resolves | where it stands |
| `own` | its own value only, nothing inherited | `bounds`, `surface`, `layout`, `at` |
| `addsUp` | the sum along the whole chain | `z`, `angle` |
| `multiplies` | the product along the whole chain | `scale` |
| `fromOwner` | the nearest value set up the chain | no field yet |
| `rootOnly` | the field does not exist on a child; asking is meaningless | no field yet |
The last two are written and waiting for a field — `nearestAlongChain` is there, ready. Worth
knowing in advance: a rule invented on the day it is first needed usually turns out to be a
fourth variety of `own`.
**`at` is `own`, and that is the least obvious row.** A position is not inherited: a card in a
hand does not ACQUIRE the hand's coordinate, it simply stands inside it, and where is the
owner's layout's business. Add them and the card would be off by the sum of two offsets.
**`scale` multiplies rather than adds,** and it is why the class exists at all. The neutral value
here is one, not zero: a half inside a half is a quarter, and no sum says that. Add them instead
and a node nobody said a word about would come out with no size at all.
## The class is declared beside the field
```ts
export const Transformable = defineAtom<TransformableFields>({
name: "Transformable",
defaults: { at: { x: 0, y: 0 }, z: 0, angle: 0, scale: 1 },
classes: { at: "own", z: "addsUp", angle: "addsUp", scale: "multiplies" },
Not in a table off to one side, but in the atom itself — and `defineAtom` checks it at
declaration: a field with no class, or a class for no field, fails the registration on the spot.
A rule about a field has to live where the field lives, or the two drift, and the drift is quiet.
## Read at apply time
None of these numbers may be remembered.
```ts
remove(hand, card)
add(desk, card)
resolveZ(contextFor(card, host.unit()))   // now 2, not 12
Move the card and the next frame knows the new number, with nothing to invalidate, because
nothing was ever stored.
In the first client this broke the order of cards in a fan three separate times: an animation
captured the base `z` when a flight began, and the fan could collapse while the card was still
in the air. The card landed under its own shadow — which looked like a bug in the shadows rather
than a frozen number.
## Notes
- The context also carries the viewer's plane, so a node never has to be ASKED about the
onlooker. It cascades the same way and never travels: two players hold different values over
one truth.
- A node that said nothing about a field does not take part: nothing in a sum, one in a product.
docs.engine.baking: A plan hands the renderer two things at once: a contour in the node's **own** coordinates, and a
**matrix** saying where that space lands on the glass. There are two ways to consume the pair,
and they differ in exactly one visible thing: a **stroke**.
**Live** — the renderer applies the matrix. One matrix per object is what a GPU does for free,
so a card that spins uploads no new geometry. The cost is that a matrix scales EVERYTHING it
touches: at twice the size the border is twice as thick and the dashes twice as long.
**Baked** — the matrix is folded into the points here, in a pure function, and the renderer gets
the identity. The border keeps the weight it was authored with and the dash pattern is cut
again along the longer contour — the same dashes, more of them. This is what SVG spells
`vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke`. The cost is recomputing it on every frame the node moves.
**Live for what moves, baked for what does not.** For a dashed border it is not an optimisation
but the correct answer: a dash is an operation on a contour, and stretching it like a picture is
the exact defect the dash rules were written against.
The node says which it is, by carrying `Bakeable`:
```ts
node("zone", Bounded(), Surfaced(), Bakeable())   // rests; fold it
node("card", Bounded(), Surfaced())               // moves; hand it a matrix
No fields on it — presence declares it, absence declines it. A whole scene is overruled at the
painter, which takes a predicate rather than a switch, because the three settings worth naming
turned out to be three special cases of one function and the interesting ones were not among
them:
```ts
attachPainter(host, painter)                                    // ask each node (the default)
attachPainter(host, painter, { bake: () => true })              // everyone
attachPainter(host, painter, { bake: () => false })             // nobody
attachPainter(host, painter, { bake: (n) => bakeable(n) && !flying.has(n.id) })
It is handed the NODE, never an id: an id is a name, and naming every card in order to say
"bake the cards" is bookkeeping the kit should not impose.
Nothing here sticks. The plan is rebuilt from scratch on every redraw, so baking is a decision
per frame rather than a state — flip it and the next frame is different, with no cache to
invalidate. And the answer this is heading for is automatic: bake whatever is not moving. The
kit will be able to say that itself the day movement is an atom, and it is the same sentence,
so nothing written today has to change.
One thing baking cannot do: fold a rotation into a node that carries a **picture**. A layer's
picture is a rect — `x, y, w, h`, aligned to the screen axes — with nowhere to write an angle,
so a turned card would come out with a turned frame and a straight face. Such a quad stays live
however firmly it was asked for. Points have no such trouble, so a turned node made of fill and
stroke alone is baked normally.
docs.engine.bakingScene: **The difference, on one canvas.** Left carries `Bakeable`, right does not. Same shape, same
surface, same pose — and the borders are not the same border: left keeps the weight and dash
pattern it was authored with, right has both multiplied by the matrix.
Take `scale` back to 1 and the two become pixel-identical. Without a scale there is nothing to
see, and the choice is purely about cost.
`policy` is the painter's own say. **asked** passes no option at all — the kit's default, which
is to ask each node. **all** and **none** overrule the tree, and are the two dullest members of
the family of predicates the option really accepts.
Turn `angle` and who bakes does not change: neither node carries a picture, and points do not
mind a rotation. The refusal in the prose above is about a picture, not about an angle — this
is the case that shows the difference between the two.
docs.engine.records: Three ways to get something ready-made out of the kit, and they are not interchangeable. A **preset** is a function that returns data, and you write it into the node's field yourself. A **record** is data sitting in a registry under a name, and the node refers to it by STRING. An **assembly** is a function returning a ready piece of tree. Which of the three you are holding shows in what ends up on the node: a value, a name, or the node itself.

`rect(1, 1.4)` and `star(5, 1, 0.42)` return a `Shape` — it goes into `Bounded({ bounds })`. `fan(5)`, `stack(12)`, `cascade(7)` return a pose per card — you spread them over the children's `Transformable`. These are ORDINARY functions: no registry, no registration, no special status. The layers below never heard of them — delete `src/presets/` and the core and the renderer keep working.
Which is why your own preset is simply a new function with the same answer type:
export function diamond(w: number, h: number): Shape {
Poses obey the same law layouts do: a `DealtPose` is `at` and `angle`, and the TYPE has no room for a `z` or a scale. A fan that lifted every card would raise a lifted hand twice.
## A record: data in a registry, referenced by name

`Surfaced({ surface: "plate" })` and `Container({ layout: "row" })` carry no paint layers and no placing function — only a string. The registry answers for the string at paint or placement time, not at tree-building time. Everything a preset cannot do follows from that:
- **one record — many nodes**: re-register `plate` and every wearer repaints, with no tree walk — that is what a skin is;
- **the tree does not haul looks around**: a name travels the wire, not layers and strokes;
- **an unknown name skips one node, it does not take the scene down**: the artist mistyped a string, not broke the desk.

The stock records are not special modes but the same kind of registry tenant: `plate`, `bare`, `zone`, `ink`, `mark`, `trail` are installed by `installStockSurfaces()`, `free` and `row` by `installStockLayouts()`. Both by the consumer's call, not on import: a module with a side effect is a module whose import order starts to matter.
A surface record is layers bottom-first, a corner radius, and a stroke over everything; tokens come from the palette, lengths are in units:
An empty `layers` is legal — a record that only strokes its contour: that is how `ink` and `trail` are built, and the whole difference between them is the record's `dash`, not the geometry.

A layout record is one method: `place(children)` returns an answer per child, IN THE SAME ORDER. A point means "I put this one here"; `undefined` means "not mine to place — its own `at` stands". The entire difference between the stock layouts is in that answer:
// free answers undefined to everyone — a "canvas" is a layout that declines to place:
// row answers a point to everyone: measures footprints, centres the sum, walks a cursor.
Your own layout registers with the same gesture a surface does:

What a layout record MAY say is points only: `place`'s answer has no `z`, no angle, no scale — a canon the type itself holds. `gap` and `padding` are parameters of the RECORD, not fields of the container: a gap means something in a row and nothing in a free layout, and a field four arrangements out of five cannot read is a field that gets misread. And a layout writes nothing back into the nodes: on the glass its answer beats the child's own `at`, but the field itself is untouched — switch `row` back to `free` and the cards come home.

Preset and record meet in `rowLayout({ gap, padding })`: it is a preset — a function returning a RECORD, still nameless. Registration gives it the name, so your own row with a different gap is one line:

`arrow({ ... })` returns a `Node` — a run and two heads, three nodes wearing ordinary atoms. Not a new atom and not a record: a ready piece of tree that lives by the common laws from then on — walk it, repaint it, turn it like anything built by hand. Its heads take their shape from a registry of their own (`registerHead`) — an assembly stands ON both mechanisms rather than beside them.

The catalog's shelves split along exactly these three answer types: `Presets/Bounds` and `Presets/Poses` are data functions, `Presets/Surfaces` are records, `Presets/Layouts` are the bridge in shelf form (functions returning still-nameless records), `Presets/Components` are assemblies.
